questions.stem: A student lists four conditions. Which one is a non-infectious disease?
options: Influenza
Tuberculosis
Malaria
Type 2 diabetes
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes arises from a combination of lifestyle and genetic factors affecting insulin action, with no pathogen involved, so it cannot be transmitted. Malaria is the most tempting distractor because it is spread by mosquitoes rather than person to person, but it is still caused by a pathogen (a Plasmodium protozoan) and is therefore infectious. The test is whether a living agent causes it, not how it travels.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a quarantine protocol?
options: Prescribing a course of antibiotics to a patient with a bacterial throat infection
Running television advertisements explaining how a disease spreads
Requiring travellers exposed to an outbreak to stay isolated for the incubation period
Washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after using the toilet
questions.explanation: Quarantine means separating people who may have been exposed, so that if they do become infectious they cannot pass the pathogen on. Handwashing is a personal hygiene measure — it removes pathogens from the body's surfaces but does not separate people. Antibiotics are medical treatment and advertising is public education; each is a distinct control category in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Which pairing of pathogen type and disease is correct?
options: Bacterium — chickenpox
Protozoan — the common cold
Fungus — tinea (athlete's foot)
Virus — tetanus
questions.explanation: Tinea is a fungal infection of the skin, so fungus and tinea is the correct pairing. Bacterium with chickenpox is tempting because chickenpox produces obvious skin lesions that look infected, but it is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Tetanus is bacterial and the common cold is viral, so both of those pairings are wrong too.

questions.stem: A school has an outbreak of gastroenteritis spread by the faecal-oral route. Which measure most directly interrupts this transmission pathway?
options: Increasing ventilation by opening classroom windows
Applying insect repellent before outdoor lessons
Thorough handwashing with soap after toileting and before eating
Asking students to cover coughs and sneezes with their elbow
questions.explanation: Faecal-oral transmission means pathogens travel from faeces to the mouth, usually on hands or contaminated food, so handwashing at those two moments breaks the chain. Covering coughs is a genuine hygiene measure but targets droplet spread, which is not how this outbreak is moving. Match the control measure to the actual route of transmission, not just to 'good hygiene' in general.

questions.stem: Why can a person be required to quarantine even though they feel completely well?
options: Quarantine is used to build immunity in healthy people before they meet the pathogen
Feeling well proves the immune system has cleared the pathogen, so quarantine is only a formality
Pathogens only become dangerous after a person has been isolated from others for several days
Many pathogens have an incubation period during which a person can be infectious before symptoms appear
questions.explanation: The incubation period is the time between infection and the appearance of symptoms, and for many diseases a person can shed pathogens during part of it, so symptom-free people can still spread disease. The option saying feeling well proves clearance is tempting because we usually judge illness by symptoms, but the absence of symptoms says nothing reliable about whether a pathogen is replicating. Remember that quarantine targets possible infection, while isolation targets confirmed infection.

questions.stem: A doctor explains that antibiotics will not help a patient's illness and that overusing them causes harm. Which statement is scientifically correct?
options: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, and overuse selects for resistant bacterial strains
Antibiotics act on all pathogens, but overuse makes the patient's immune system permanently weaker
Antibiotics act on viruses only, so bacterial infections must instead be treated with vaccines
Antibiotics act on bacteria, but resistance develops because individual bacteria deliberately change to survive
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target structures and processes found in bacteria, such as cell walls, which viruses lack; when antibiotics are used often, the few bacteria that already carry resistance survive and reproduce, so resistant strains become common. The option about bacteria deliberately changing is tempting because resistance does emerge from antibiotic use, but bacteria cannot choose to mutate — variation exists first and the drug selects it. Keep 'selection of existing variation' as the mechanism, never intent.

questions.stem: Mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite between people. What is that role called?
options: A pathogen, because it is the organism that causes the illness
A reservoir, because the parasite's whole life cycle is in mosquitoes
A host response, because the bite triggers the immune system
A vector, an organism carrying the pathogen from one host to another
questions.explanation: A vector is an organism, usually an insect, that transfers a pathogen between hosts without being the cause of the disease itself; here the pathogen is the Plasmodium parasite. Calling the mosquito a pathogen is the common slip — students say 'mosquitoes cause malaria', but remove the parasite and the bite causes no malaria. The cue: ask what would still make you sick if it were present, and that is the pathogen.

questions.stem: Two Year 10 students argue about lung cancer. Which statement about its classification is correct?
options: It is infectious, because smoke particles containing the causative agent can be breathed in by others
It is non-infectious only in non-smokers, since smoking-related cases spread through shared air
It is infectious, because families in which several members smoke often show several cases
It is non-infectious, because it results from damage to cell DNA and cannot be passed to another person
questions.explanation: Lung cancer arises when mutations accumulate in the DNA of lung cells, most often from carcinogens in tobacco smoke; there is no pathogen and no transmission between hosts, so it is non-infectious. The option about clustering within families is the trap: shared behaviour and shared environment produce clusters that look like spread, but no agent passes from person to person. Passive smoking does raise risk in others, yet that is exposure to a chemical cause, not infection.

questions.stem: During an influenza outbreak, health authorities use vaccination, isolation of sick people and handwashing campaigns together rather than relying on any single measure. What is the main scientific reason for combining them?
options: Each measure interrupts transmission at a different point, so gaps left by one are covered by the others
Combining measures makes the virus mutate more slowly, which stops the outbreak spreading
Using several measures together makes the immune system produce more antibodies than vaccination alone
Each measure only works on some strains, so several are needed to cover every strain in circulation
questions.explanation: Control measures act at different stages — vaccination reduces susceptibility, isolation removes infectious people from contact, and hygiene removes pathogens from hands and surfaces — so layering them leaves fewer routes open. The claim about extra antibodies confuses immune response with transmission control; handwashing has no effect on antibody production. Mutation rate is driven by viral replication, not by whether people wash their hands.

questions.stem: A student claims that because stomach ulcers were once blamed on stress and spicy food, all diseases once thought non-infectious are really infectious. Most stomach ulcers are in fact caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. What does this example actually show?
options: Classification depends on evidence about the cause, so a disease may be reclassified when a pathogen is identified
Non-infectious diseases do not really exist, since every condition will eventually be traced to a microbe
Stress and diet cause no disease at all, because bacterial causes always turn out to be the real explanation
Ulcers are both infectious and non-infectious, because bacteria and stress cause identical damage to tissue
questions.explanation: Whether a disease is infectious is decided by evidence about its cause, and the ulcer case shows that better evidence can move a disease from one category to the other. It does not follow that all non-infectious diseases hide a pathogen — conditions such as inherited cystic fibrosis and injury-related disease have well-established non-pathogenic causes. Diet and lifestyle factors remain genuine contributors to many non-infectious diseases, so dismissing them entirely overreaches the evidence.

questions.stem: Tinea (athlete's foot) produces itchy, flaking skin between the toes and spreads on damp change-room floors. Which type of organism causes it?
options: A fungus
A bacterium
A virus
A protozoan
questions.explanation: Tinea is a fungal infection of the skin, which is why it thrives in warm, moist conditions and is treated with antifungal creams rather than antibiotics. The most tempting wrong answer is bacterium, because students often assume any skin infection that spreads by contact is bacterial; antibiotics have no effect on tinea. A useful cue is that fungal infections typically affect warm, damp surfaces such as feet, skin folds and nails.

questions.stem: Sailors got scurvy because their diet lacked vitamin C. How should scurvy be classified?
options: Infectious, because it spread through contaminated food and water on board
Non-infectious, because it is caused by a bacterium that grows in the poorly fed
Non-infectious, because it comes from a nutritional deficiency, not a pathogen
Infectious, because it appeared in many crew living in the same crowded quarters
questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by the absence of a required nutrient, so there is no pathogen to pass between people and it is non-infectious. The most tempting distractor is the one pointing to many crew members falling ill at once, but shared conditions can produce many cases of a non-infectious disease without any transmission occurring. Many people getting sick together shows a shared cause, not necessarily a contagious one.

questions.stem: Dengue fever is caused by a virus carried between people by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in small pools of still water. Which control measure most directly interrupts this transmission pathway?
options: Boiling or chlorinating all drinking water supplied to the community
Asking people with a cough to wear a fitted mask in crowded indoor spaces
Emptying pot plant saucers, buckets and blocked gutters around homes each week
Encouraging thorough handwashing with soap before preparing and eating meals
questions.explanation: Because the virus can only reach a new person through a mosquito, removing the standing water where mosquitoes breed cuts the number of vectors and breaks the chain of transmission. Boiling drinking water is tempting because water is mentioned, but dengue is not spread by drinking contaminated water — the water simply provides a mosquito nursery. Match the control measure to how the pathogen actually travels between hosts.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a public education program used to control infectious disease?
options: Border officers requiring arrivals to spend 14 days in a supervised hotel
A pharmacist supplying antibiotics prescribed for a bacterial infection
A government campaign teaching people how and when to wash their hands
A hospital placing a measles patient in a room away from other patients
questions.explanation: Public education programs work by changing the behaviour of large numbers of people through information — advertising, school lessons, posters and health messaging. Placing a measles patient in a separate room is isolation, a quarantine-type protocol, which is tempting because it is also a public health action but it physically separates people rather than informing them. Supplying antibiotics is medical treatment, and hotel quarantine is a quarantine protocol. The cue is whether the measure works by teaching or by separating and treating.

questions.stem: Which group of diseases are all non-infectious?
options: Type 2 diabetes, asthma and coronary heart disease
Tuberculosis, asthma and type 2 diabetes
Coronary heart disease, chickenpox and osteoarthritis
Anaemia from iron deficiency, tetanus and melanoma
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes, asthma and coronary heart disease all arise from combinations of genetics, lifestyle and environment, and none is spread from person to person. Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, chickenpox by the varicella-zoster virus and tetanus by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, so any list containing them is not all non-infectious. The list with tuberculosis is the most tempting because the other two conditions are chronic and non-infectious — check every item, not just the first two.

questions.stem: A surgeon scrubs her hands, wears sterile gloves and uses instruments that have been through an autoclave. Which transmission route are these measures mainly designed to block?
options: Transmission by an insect vector such as a mosquito or tick
Faecal-oral spread of pathogens through contaminated drinking water
Entry of pathogens directly into body tissues through the surgical wound
Airborne spread of pathogens between patients in the waiting room
questions.explanation: Surgery breaks the skin, removing the body's main physical barrier, so sterile technique is aimed at stopping micro-organisms on hands and instruments from entering the wound and tissues directly. Airborne spread is the most tempting alternative because masks are also worn in theatre, but gloves and autoclaved instruments target contact with the wound rather than droplets in a waiting room. Match each measure to the specific barrier or route it acts on.

questions.stem: Cholera cases in a region fell sharply after piped, treated water and sealed sewers were installed, well before any specific medical treatment was widely available. What does this best illustrate?
options: Cholera must therefore be a non-infectious disease caused by poor living conditions rather than a pathogen
Interrupting a pathogen's transmission route can reduce disease incidence even without treating individual patients
The cholera bacterium mutated into a harmless form once the water supply was cleaned and sewers were sealed
People in the region developed inherited immunity to cholera that was passed on to their children
questions.explanation: Cholera spreads by the faecal-oral route, so removing contaminated water from the pathway between an infected person's waste and another person's mouth stops new infections regardless of how existing cases are treated. The idea that this makes cholera non-infectious is tempting because environment clearly matters, but the cause is still the bacterium Vibrio cholerae — the environment only determines how easily it reaches new hosts. Immunity to a pathogen acquired during life is not inherited by offspring.

questions.stem: Which action is personal hygiene, rather than quarantine, treatment or education?
options: Taking a full course of prescribed antibiotics until they are finished
Running advertisements showing families how flu spreads at home
Covering your mouth and nose with your elbow when you cough
Staying home for a set number of days after leaving an outbreak area
questions.explanation: Personal hygiene refers to what an individual does with their own body and belongings to stop pathogens spreading, such as covering coughs, washing hands and not sharing drink bottles. The antibiotic course is medical treatment: it kills the pathogen in an already infected patient rather than blocking its escape from the body. Cue: hygiene measures act at the moment a pathogen could leave or enter a body.

questions.stem: On a windy spring day, six students at one school have asthma attacks within a few hours. How should asthma be classified, and why?
options: Non-infectious, because asthma is caused purely by inherited genes and is never affected by the environment
Infectious, because several people in the same place developed the same symptoms at almost the same time
Non-infectious, because the attacks were triggered by pollen and no pathogen moved from one student to another
Infectious, because the trigger was airborne and airborne conditions are always spread from person to person
questions.explanation: Asthma is a non-infectious condition of the airways; pollen is an irritant and allergen, not a reproducing pathogen, so nothing was transmitted between students. The 'several people at once' option is the strongest trap, but a shared environmental trigger produces clustered cases without any transmission. Note also that asthma is not purely genetic — environmental triggers clearly matter, which makes that option false even though its conclusion sounds right.

questions.stem: Health authorities set the length of a quarantine period for a newly emerging infectious disease. What determines how many days it should last?
options: The longest usual incubation period, so an infected person will develop symptoms before mixing with others
The time an antibiotic course takes to work, so treatment is finished before the person leaves quarantine
The length of time the pathogen can survive on hard surfaces such as door handles and benches
The time a vaccine takes to produce antibodies, so the person is immune by the end of quarantine
questions.explanation: Quarantine separates people who may have been exposed but are not yet known to be infected, so it must be long enough to cover the incubation period — the gap between infection and symptoms appearing. The surface-survival option confuses cleaning and disinfection timeframes with the biology happening inside an exposed person. Cue: quarantine is about waiting out the incubation period, not about treatment, vaccines or surfaces.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between an infectious and a non-infectious disease?
options: An infectious disease is inherited from parents; a non-infectious one is environmental
An infectious disease can be treated with medicines; a non-infectious one cannot
An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen that passes between hosts
An infectious disease is always more severe and faster; a non-infectious one is slow
questions.explanation: The classification depends on cause and transmissibility: infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, some worms) that can be passed between hosts, whereas non-infectious diseases arise from genetic, lifestyle, nutritional or environmental factors and cannot be caught. The option about severity and speed is tempting because many infections do come on quickly, but plenty of infections are mild or long-lasting (such as tinea) and many non-infectious conditions, like anaphylaxis, strike within minutes. Ask 'can it be passed to someone else?' rather than 'how bad or how fast is it?'.

questions.stem: Which type of infectious agent is not made of cells and can only reproduce inside a living host cell?
options: A fungus
A protozoan
A virus
A bacterium
questions.explanation: Viruses are non-cellular particles made of genetic material inside a protein coat; they have no cell machinery of their own and must hijack a host cell to make copies. Bacteria are the most tempting wrong answer because they are microscopic and cause many familiar illnesses, but each bacterium is a complete cell that can grow and divide on its own, for example on agar in a petri dish. The cue is independent reproduction: only viruses cannot reproduce outside a host cell.

questions.stem: Which of these actions is an example of medical treatment as a way of controlling infectious disease, rather than hygiene, quarantine or public education?
options: Washing hands with soap for twenty seconds before handling food
Prescribing a patient a full course of antiviral medication
Requiring recent overseas arrivals to stay home for ten days
Running radio advertisements about covering coughs and sneezes
questions.explanation: Medical treatment means using medicines or clinical care to reduce the pathogen load in an infected person, which also lowers the chance they pass it on. Requiring recent arrivals to stay home is the most tempting alternative, but separating people who may have been exposed is quarantine, not treatment, because no medicine is given. Sort each measure by asking what is actually being done: given a drug, separated, cleaned, or informed.

questions.stem: Staff at a childcare centre wipe down toys, tabletops and door handles with disinfectant every afternoon. Which route of transmission are they mainly trying to interrupt?
options: Vertical spread, where a pathogen passes from mother to baby before birth
Indirect contact, where pathogens are picked up from contaminated objects
Airborne spread, where pathogens drift long distances in the air
Vector-borne spread, where an insect carries pathogens between people
questions.explanation: Objects such as toys and handles are fomites: a sick child leaves pathogens on the surface, another child touches it and then their mouth or eyes, so cleaning breaks that link. Airborne spread is tempting because respiratory infections are common in childcare, but disinfecting surfaces does nothing to particles suspended in the air, which need ventilation or masks instead. Match the measure to the place the pathogen sits: surfaces mean indirect contact.

questions.stem: Forty people who attended the same community picnic developed vomiting and cramps within about twelve hours, while no one else in the town became ill that week. Which conclusion is best supported by this pattern?
options: The illness must have spread person to person over several weeks of close contact
The illness must be inherited, because the cases were clustered in one group of people
A common source, most likely contaminated food or drink at the picnic, caused the outbreak
The illness must be non-infectious, because only people at one event became unwell
questions.explanation: A tight cluster of cases with a short, similar time to onset, all linked to one shared event, is the classic signature of a point-source outbreak from contaminated food or water. Saying it must be non-infectious is tempting because outsiders stayed well, but a single contaminated source infects only those exposed to it and the agent is still a pathogen. Look at timing: symptoms within hours of one shared exposure point to a common source, not to slow person-to-person chains.

questions.stem: During an outbreak, a health department uses both isolation and quarantine. What is the difference between them?
options: Quarantine applies only to imported animals and goods, while isolation applies only to human patients
Isolation separates people known to be infected, while quarantine separates well people who may have been exposed
Quarantine separates people with confirmed symptoms, while isolation separates well people who may have been exposed
Isolation is only used at international borders, while quarantine is only used inside hospitals
questions.explanation: Isolation keeps confirmed or symptomatic cases away from others so they cannot pass the pathogen on, while quarantine restricts apparently well contacts for the length of the incubation period in case they later become infectious. The reversed version of this statement is the common trap, because both terms simply sound like 'staying away from people'. The cue is infection status: known infection means isolation, possible exposure means quarantine.

questions.stem: In the study of disease, what is a pathogen?
options: An inherited fault in a gene that causes a disease to develop over time
An organism or agent, such as a bacterium or virus, that causes disease in a host
A protein made by the body that sticks to invading microbes and marks them
A white blood cell that engulfs and digests microbes that enter the body
questions.explanation: A pathogen is any disease-causing organism or agent — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and some worms — that infects a host. The description of a protein that sticks to invading microbes is an antibody, which is part of the body's defence against pathogens, not the pathogen itself. A useful cue: pathogens attack the body from outside; antibodies and white blood cells are the body's own defenders.

questions.stem: Which infectious agent consists of single cells that have no nucleus and can often be treated with antibiotics?
options: Protozoa
Bacteria
Viruses
Fungi
questions.explanation: Bacteria are single-celled organisms without a nucleus (prokaryotes), and antibiotics work by attacking bacterial structures such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses are the most tempting alternative, but they are not made of cells at all — they are genetic material in a protein coat — and antibiotics have no effect on them. Fungi and protozoa are made of cells that do have nuclei, and are treated with antifungal or antiparasitic medicines instead.

questions.stem: Why does washing hands thoroughly with soap and running water reduce the spread of infectious disease?
options: Warm soapy water raises skin temperature enough to kill pathogens by heat alone
Soap loosens microbes and oily grime from the skin so running water rinses them away
Soap sterilises the skin, killing every microbe present and keeping hands germ-free all day
Soap triggers the skin to release antibodies that destroy pathogens on contact
questions.explanation: Soap molecules break up oils and disrupt the fatty membranes of many microbes, lifting them from the skin so they are physically carried away by the rinse water. The 'sterilises the skin' option is tempting because washing clearly helps, but hands are recontaminated within minutes and normal washing never removes all microbes. The cue is that handwashing mainly removes pathogens rather than killing them, which is why the rinsing step matters as much as the soap.

questions.stem: Three members of one family have been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. A student concludes that the disease must be catching. Which response is scientifically correct?
options: Disease clustering within a household is always evidence that an infectious agent is involved
Shared genes and a shared lifestyle explain the clustering; no pathogen passes between family members
The clustering shows a slow bacterium is spreading between family members over many years
Diabetes spreads between people through shared meals and utensils rather than through the air
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is non-infectious: families share inherited risk genes as well as diet, activity patterns and body weight, so cases can cluster without anything being transmitted. The suggestion of a slow-spreading bacterium is wrong because no pathogen has any role in type 2 diabetes. The cue is to ask whether an infectious agent can be identified — clustering alone can also come from shared genetics or shared environment.

questions.stem: A baby is too young to receive the measles vaccine, yet is well protected while living in a district with a very high vaccination rate. What best explains this protection?
options: Antibodies pass from vaccinated people to the baby through everyday contact such as handling
Being surrounded by immune people makes the baby's own immune system mature more quickly
With few susceptible people around, chains of transmission break down, so the baby is rarely exposed
Vaccinated neighbours breathe out weakened vaccine virus that immunises the baby harmlessly
questions.explanation: When most people in a community are immune, an infected person is unlikely to meet a susceptible contact, so outbreaks fizzle out and unvaccinated individuals are indirectly protected — this is herd immunity. The idea that antibodies pass between people through everyday contact is wrong: antibodies are only transferred across the placenta, through breast milk, or by medical injection. The cue is that herd immunity works by reducing exposure, not by giving the unvaccinated person immunity.

questions.stem: A new illness appears in a country town. Which observation would give the strongest evidence that it is infectious rather than non-infectious?
options: Most patients report that their symptoms ease after several days of rest and fluids
The illness appeared during an unusually hot and humid stretch of summer weather
New cases keep appearing among people who spent time with those who fell ill earlier
All the people affected so far are over sixty years of age and live in the same town
questions.explanation: A pattern in which cases follow contact with earlier cases, spaced by a consistent interval, points to an agent being passed from person to person — the defining feature of an infectious disease. Cases sharing an age group and a location is tempting, but that pattern equally fits a non-infectious cause such as a shared environmental exposure or a diet-related condition. The cue is to look for transmission between people, not just for cases sharing a characteristic.

questions.stem: A patient with a bacterial throat infection is prescribed antibiotics and told to complete the whole course. Besides curing that patient, how does this treatment help control transmission in the community?
options: It changes the bacteria into a harmless form that can no longer live in other people
It reduces the number of bacteria the patient carries and sheds, so fewer people are exposed
It makes the surrounding community immune to the same bacteria through shared exposure
It kills the bacteria in everyone the patient has already met, ending the outbreak
questions.explanation: Medical treatment shortens the infectious period by lowering the pathogen load a sick person carries and sheds, so there are fewer bacteria available to pass on. The option about the community becoming immune confuses treatment with vaccination or herd immunity, which requires people's own immune systems to respond. The cue is that antibiotics act only inside the person taking them.

questions.stem: Airport staff arriving from an area with an outbreak of a respiratory virus wear fitted masks. Which transmission route is a mask primarily designed to interrupt?
options: Vector-borne spread, by preventing biting insects from reaching the face
Contaminated food and water spread, by filtering pathogens out of what is swallowed
Direct contact spread, by preventing skin-to-skin touching between people
Airborne and droplet spread of the pathogen when people breathe, cough or speak
questions.explanation: Masks form a barrier over the nose and mouth, so they act on droplets and fine airborne particles released and inhaled during breathing, coughing and speaking. Direct contact spread is the tempting distractor, but skin-to-skin transmission is interrupted by handwashing and gloves, not by a face covering. Match each control measure to the specific route it physically blocks.

questions.stem: Head lice, tapeworms and scabies mites are all agents of disease in humans. Which group do they belong to?
options: Fungi, which absorb nutrients from the host's tissues
Multicellular parasites that live on or inside a host organism
Bacteria, which are single cells without a true nucleus
Viruses, which can only reproduce inside living host cells
questions.explanation: Lice, worms and mites are multicellular animals that live on or in a host and take nutrients from it, so they are classed as parasites rather than microbes. Choosing bacteria is a common slip because students group all disease agents as 'germs', but bacteria are single cells far too small to be seen, whereas lice and mites are visible animals with legs. If the agent is a visible organism with body parts, it is a parasite, not a microbe.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis occurs when a child inherits a faulty version of a particular gene from both parents. How should this disease be classified, and why?
options: Infectious, because the faulty gene acts like a pathogen inside the child's cells
Non-infectious, because the cause is a faulty gene rather than a pathogen entering the body
Infectious, because it is passed from parents to their child in the family
Non-infectious, because it is caused by lifestyle choices such as diet and exercise
questions.explanation: Infectious diseases require a pathogen — a living agent or virus — to be transmitted into a host, while cystic fibrosis results from inherited DNA, so it is non-infectious and genetic. The answer saying it is infectious because it passes from parents to child is the trap: genes are inherited at conception, not transmitted like a microbe, and a person with cystic fibrosis cannot give it to a classmate. Ask whether the cause could spread to an unrelated person by contact; if not, it is non-infectious.

questions.stem: A cafe worker uses one chopping board only for raw chicken, washes her hands with soap after handling it, and never lets raw juices touch salad ingredients. Which category of infectious disease control do these actions best fit?
options: Public education, which changes community behaviour through information campaigns
Personal and food hygiene, which reduces the chance of pathogens reaching a new host
Quarantine protocols, which separate exposed people from the rest of the community
Medical treatment, which removes pathogens already growing inside a patient
questions.explanation: Hygiene measures work by physically removing or separating pathogens so they never reach a new host, which is exactly what handwashing and separate boards achieve. Public education is the most tempting alternative, but education means the program that teaches safe practices, not the individual worker carrying them out at the bench. Match the measure to who is acting: an individual removing germs is hygiene, while a health department informing many people is education.

questions.stem: A country town records an unusual cluster of mesothelioma, a lung disease, among former workers at one old factory. No family members or newer residents are affected. What does this pattern best show?
options: An infectious disease with a long incubation period that only affects adult workers
A non-infectious disease caused by a shared environmental exposure at the workplace
An infectious disease, because a group of people in one place developed the same illness
A non-infectious disease that has recently become able to spread between close contacts
questions.explanation: Clusters can arise either from transmission or from many people sharing an exposure; here the cases are confined to workers at one site and do not appear in their households, which points to an environmental agent such as asbestos fibres rather than a spreading pathogen. Calling it infectious because a group in one place fell ill is the main trap — a cluster alone is not evidence of transmission. Look for spread to contacts and new arrivals: without that, a shared exposure is the better explanation.

questions.stem: What is a pathogen?
options: A cell that fights infection
A chemical that kills bacteria
A protein made by the liver
An organism that causes disease
questions.explanation: Pathogens are disease-causing organisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites. A cell that fights infection is a white blood cell, which is on the opposite side of the same story.
questions.teaching:
It is worth separating the things that cause disease from the things that fight it, because both come up in the same questions.

On the causing side are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa — organisms that invade the body and either damage tissue directly or release toxins. On the fighting side are white blood cells and the proteins they produce. Note that not all disease has a cause of this kind: scurvy comes from a missing vitamin, and diabetes from a failure of glucose control. Those are non-infectious, which is precisely why the definition here matters.

questions.stem: Which of these is caused by a virus?
options: Tuberculosis
Scurvy
Influenza
Tetanus
questions.explanation: Influenza is viral. Tetanus and tuberculosis are bacterial, and scurvy is not infectious at all — it comes from a lack of vitamin C.
questions.teaching:
Sorting diseases by what causes them is worth doing, because it determines what treatment can work.

Bacteria are living cells, and antibiotics can kill them. Tuberculosis, tetanus and strep throat are all bacterial. Viruses are not cells at all — they are genetic material in a protein coat that hijacks your cells to copy themselves — and antibiotics do nothing to them. Colds, measles, chickenpox and the flu are viral, which is why vaccination matters so much for these. And some diseases are not infectious at all, such as scurvy, which is a dietary deficiency.

questions.stem: What do vaccines do?
options: Train the immune system before infection
Kill pathogens already in the blood
Replace nutrients missing from the diet
Reduce a fever once it has started
questions.explanation: A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen so memory cells are ready in advance. It is preparation, not treatment, which is why killing pathogens already present is the wrong answer.
questions.teaching:
A vaccine is not a treatment. It does nothing for an infection you already have, and that distinction is what most questions here test.

What it does is show the immune system a harmless version of a pathogen first — weakened, inactivated, or just a fragment such as a surface protein. The body responds as it would to a real infection, producing antibodies and, crucially, memory cells. Those memory cells persist. If the real pathogen arrives later, the response is fast enough to stop illness developing. So the whole point is preparation in advance, which is why timing matters.

questions.stem: What are antibodies?
options: Chemicals that lower body temperature
Sugars stored in the liver for energy
Proteins that bind to specific pathogens
Cells that swallow and digest bacteria
questions.explanation: Antibodies are proteins shaped to lock onto one particular pathogen, marking it for destruction. Cells that swallow bacteria are phagocytes — also part of immunity, but cells rather than proteins.
questions.teaching:
The immune system uses several tools, and it helps to keep the cells and the molecules apart.

Some white blood cells engulf and digest invaders directly. Others produce Y-shaped proteins with a binding site shaped to fit one particular pathogen's surface and nothing else. That specificity is the key feature: the ones made for measles do nothing against chickenpox. Once bound, they mark the invader for destruction and can stop it entering cells. Because production speeds up dramatically on a second exposure, this is also the mechanism vaccination is exploiting.

questions.stem: What does an antibiotic treat?
options: Viral infections
Genetic conditions
Vitamin deficiencies
Bacterial infections
questions.explanation: Antibiotics work on bacteria and do nothing against viruses. Taking them for a cold is both useless and a driver of resistance, which is why this distinction matters beyond the exam.
questions.teaching:
Antibiotics work by attacking structures that bacteria have and human cells do not — cell walls, in particular. That is what makes them safe for us and lethal to bacteria.

Viruses have none of those structures. They are not cells, and they replicate inside your own cells, so there is nothing for the drug to attack. Taking antibiotics for a cold or the flu therefore achieves nothing medically while still killing off harmless bacteria and giving resistant strains an opening. This is not a technicality — it is the single biggest driver of antibiotic resistance, which is why doctors decline to prescribe them for viral illness.

questions.stem: What is the skin's main role in defence?
options: Absorbing nutrients from the air
A physical barrier keeping pathogens out
Producing antibodies against pathogens
Storing white blood cells for later
questions.explanation: Intact skin is a first-line barrier, which is why a cut is an infection risk. Antibody production happens in the immune system proper, not in the skin itself.
questions.teaching:
Defences are usually sorted into layers, and the first layer works before any infection has begun.

That first layer is physical and chemical rather than immune: unbroken skin that pathogens cannot cross, mucus and cilia trapping and sweeping particles out of the airways, stomach acid destroying what is swallowed, and tears containing enzymes. None of these targets a specific pathogen; they simply keep things out. The second layer — white blood cells and antibodies — only comes into play once something gets through, which is why a cut or a burn is a genuine infection risk.

questions.stem: What causes antibiotic resistance to spread?
options: People themselves developing immunity to antibiotics
Viruses learning to block the medicine
Bacteria surviving treatment and reproducing
Antibiotics becoming weaker with age
questions.explanation: Resistant bacteria survive a course of antibiotics and pass that resistance on. The tempting error is thinking the person becomes resistant — it is the bacteria that change, not the patient.
questions.teaching:
The commonest misunderstanding is that the person becomes resistant. They do not. It is the bacterial population that changes.

Random variation means a few bacteria in any large population already survive a given antibiotic. Take the drug and the susceptible ones die, leaving the survivors with no competition and plenty of room to multiply. Repeat that often enough and resistant strains dominate. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes sideways to unrelated bacteria, which speeds it up further. Finishing a prescribed course matters for exactly this reason: stopping early leaves the hardest-to-kill survivors behind.

questions.stem: What does 'herd immunity' mean?
options: Everyone in a population has been infected
Animals pass their immunity to humans
One person's immunity protects their family
Enough people are immune to slow the spread
questions.explanation: When a high enough share of a population is immune, a pathogen struggles to find new hosts, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated. It does not require everyone to be immune, only enough of them.
questions.teaching:
A pathogen spreads by finding new hosts. If most people it meets are already immune, chains of transmission keep breaking and an outbreak fizzles out.

That is the whole idea, and note what it does not require: not everyone has to be immune, only enough of them. The threshold depends on how contagious the disease is — measles is so infectious that around 95% coverage is needed, while others need far less. The point of it is protecting the people who cannot be vaccinated: newborns, people undergoing chemotherapy, and anyone with a compromised immune system.
